issues.legal_issue: Surviving co-defendants with an independent interest may prosecute an appeal from a joint decree resting on a ground common to them, even if another appellant dies during the appeal.
material_facts: The landlord obtained an eviction decree against several defendants who were in possession of the premises, on the common ground of personal requirement.
The defendants appealed jointly, and two co-defendants remained alive after the tenant died during the appeal.
The allegation that the tenant had sublet the premises was not pursued, and the eviction decree did not rest on subletting.
issues.conclusion: The appeal could not be dismissed merely because the tenant died or his heirs lacked a surviving cause of action. The surviving co-defendants had a substantial interest in prosecuting it, and the appellate courts should have heard the appeal on its merits.
issues.legal_principle: Order XLI rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits any one of multiple defendants to appeal from the whole decree when it rests on a ground common to them, and permits the appellate court to vary or reverse the decree in favour of all. Because the decree was joint and indivisible, dismissing the appeal could also risk inconsistent decrees. The Court did not need to decide whether the deceased tenant’s heirs had a surviving interest. The High Court’s reliance on Anand Nivas Private Ltd. v. Anandji Kalvanji Pedhi did not remove the surviving co-defendants’ independent right to appeal.

predicates.appeal_from_joint_decree: The proceeding is an appeal by defendants from a decree made against them jointly.
predicates.decree_based_on_common_ground: The decree rests on a ground common to the defendants appealing together.
predicates.surviving_coappellants_have_substantial_: One or more appellants remain alive and have a substantial interest in challenging the decree.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a joint decree resting on a common ground and surviving appellants have a substantial interest, the appeal must be decided on its merits.

issues.legal_issue: A person facing an eviction decree remains a tenant for purposes of the special protection governing eviction from a slum area, so a later eviction suit requires the competent authority’s prior written permission.
material_facts: The premises were in a slum area and an eviction decree had already been obtained against the occupants.
The competent authority permitted execution only for rooms on one floor and expressly refused permission for the remaining rooms.
The landlord later sued for possession of the remaining rooms without obtaining prior permission to institute that suit.
issues.conclusion: The occupants remained tenants for purposes of the Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act despite the earlier eviction decree. Because the landlord had not obtained prior permission to institute the later suit, the suit was incompetent.
issues.legal_principle: Section 19(1)(a) of the Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act requires prior written permission to institute proceedings to evict a tenant from a building in a slum area; section 19(1)(b) also restricts execution of specified earlier decrees. Section 19(4)(a), which requires consideration of whether alternative accommodation would be available to the tenant if evicted, shows that ‘tenant’ includes a person already subject to an eviction decree. The definition in section 2(1) of the Delhi Rent Control Act was not adopted for the Slum Areas Act. The Court applied the protective purpose of that Act and the rule that the same expression in a statute should ordinarily have the same meaning throughout. It followed Bardu Ram Dhanna Ram v. Ram Chander Khibru, considered Jyoti Parshad v. The Administrator for the Union Territory of Delhi, and distinguished Lakhmi Chand v. Kauran Devi.

predicates.eviction_proceeding_in_slum_area: A landlord brings a proceeding seeking to evict an occupant from premises situated in a slum area.
predicates.occupant_subject_to_eviction_decree: An eviction decree has already been made against the occupant.
predicates.prior_permission_not_obtained: The landlord has not obtained the competent authority’s prior written permission to bring the eviction proceeding.

issues.definition: An eviction suit is incompetent when it concerns a slum-area occupant subject to an eviction decree and the landlord has not obtained prior permission.

issues.legal_issue: A civil court lacks jurisdiction over a matter that the competent authority is empowered to determine under the law protecting occupants of slum areas from eviction.
material_facts: The later suit sought possession of premises in a slum area from occupants covered by an earlier eviction decree.

The competent authority was empowered to decide whether eviction proceedings could be instituted and whether the decree could be executed, and it had refused permission to execute the decree for the rooms at issue.
issues.conclusion: The suit was barred by section 37A because the question whether the occupants could be evicted was within the competent authority’s exclusive jurisdiction.
issues.legal_principle: Section 37A of the Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act excludes civil-court jurisdiction over matters that the competent authority or another person is empowered by or under the Act to determine. Under section 19, the competent authority determines whether permission should be granted for an eviction proceeding or for execution of a decree. The combined effect of sections 19 and 37A places that determination outside the civil court’s jurisdiction.

predicates.civil_court_proceeding_about_slum_evicti: The proceeding is in a civil court and concerns whether an occupant of slum-area premises may be evicted.
predicates.competent_authority_empowered_to_determi: The competent authority is empowered to decide whether the eviction proceeding or execution of the eviction decree may go forward.

issues.definition: A civil court lacks jurisdiction over a slum-eviction matter when the competent authority is empowered to decide whether eviction may go forward.

issues.legal_issue: The principle of res judicata can bar a later suit when a competent quasi-judicial tribunal has finally decided the same issue between the same parties, even if the earlier proceeding was not a suit within the terms of section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
material_facts: The landlord applied to the competent authority for permission to execute an eviction decree covering all the premises.
The authority permitted execution for some rooms but expressly refused it for the rooms later claimed in the suit, and the decision was confirmed on appeal.
The later suit involved the same parties and sought possession of the rooms for which permission had been refused.
issues.conclusion: The suit was barred by a principle analogous to res judicata because the same issue between the same parties had been finally decided by a competent quasi-judicial tribunal.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not exhaustive; its underlying principle may extend beyond proceedings that fall within its precise terms. The principle applies where the issues in the later proceeding are identical to those previously decided, the proceedings are between the same parties, and the earlier decision was final and made by a competent quasi-judicial tribunal. It is founded on public interest, equity, justice, and good conscience, and prevents repeated litigation of a decided issue.

rule.if: later_civil_suit_after_quasi_judicial_decision and same_parties and same_issue and earlier_decision_final_and_competent

predicates.later_civil_suit_after_quasi_judicial_de: A party brings a civil suit after a quasi-judicial tribunal has decided a related proceeding.
predicates.same_parties: The parties to the later suit are the same parties as those to the earlier proceeding.
predicates.same_issue: The later suit raises an issue that was also determined in the earlier proceeding.
predicates.earlier_decision_final_and_competent: A competent quasi-judicial tribunal finally decided the issue in the earlier proceeding.

issues.definition: A later suit is barred by analogous res judicata when the same parties relitigate an issue finally decided by a competent quasi-judicial tribunal.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord cannot use a fresh possession suit to obtain indirectly the part of an eviction decree that the competent authority refused to permit the landlord to execute.
material_facts: The competent authority allowed execution of the eviction decree for some rooms but refused execution for the remaining rooms.
The landlord obtained possession of the rooms covered by the permission and then brought a fresh suit seeking possession of the rooms for which execution had been refused.
issues.conclusion: The fresh suit was, in substance, an attempt to execute the eviction decree by instalments and violated the statutory restriction on execution without permission.
issues.legal_principle: Section 19(1)(b) of the Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act restricts execution of an eviction decree without the competent authority’s prior written permission. The substance, rather than the form, of the later proceeding governs: a landlord cannot evade that restriction by seeking through a fresh suit the possession that the authority had refused to allow the landlord to obtain by execution.

predicates.possession_suit_after_eviction_decree: A landlord brings a possession suit after obtaining an eviction decree against the occupant.
predicates.authority_refused_execution_for_claimed_: The competent authority refused permission to execute the decree for the premises later claimed.
predicates.suit_seeks_possession_under_same_decree: The later suit seeks substantially the same possession covered by the decree for which execution permission was refused.

issues.definition: A possession suit is impermissible indirect execution when it seeks premises covered by a decree whose execution the competent authority refused to permit.

issues.legal_issue: Occupants affected by a decree made in a suit that the civil court lacked jurisdiction to entertain may challenge the decree’s nullity to defend their possession.
material_facts: The later possession suit was incompetent because the required permission to bring it had not been obtained, and the civil court lacked jurisdiction over the matter assigned to the competent authority.
The decree was made against occupants who were entitled to rely on the statutory protection governing eviction from slum areas.
issues.conclusion: The decree was non-est, and the surviving occupants could challenge its nullity to defend and protect their possession.
issues.legal_principle: A decree made by a court without jurisdiction is a nullity. The Court held that the affected co-defendants could set up that nullity in order to defend their possession by invoking the protections of the Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act.

predicates.possession_defense_against_civil_court_d: An occupant relies on a defense in a possession dispute against a civil-court decree.
predicates.decree_made_without_jurisdiction: The civil court made the decree in a matter over which it lacked jurisdiction.
predicates.occupant_affected_by_decree: The decree affects the occupant’s possession or claimed right to remain in possession.

issues.definition: An occupant may challenge a decree as a nullity when defending possession against a decree made without jurisdiction that affects the occupant.
